premises: A padlock opened by a password key: the key gets copied and handed out, a thief opens the lock with the copy, then the key is swapped for a fingerprint and only the owner opens it.

One phone sign-in screen: the password box fails, its password is the same on every site, the same password unlocks the bank for a thief, then the box is replaced by a fingerprint and every phone signs in without one.
A race between two sign-ins: the password runner trips on typos and fake pages while the passkey runner crosses the line first, and the crowd of 5 billion passkeys cheers at the finish.
story.why: The phone sign-in screen is what viewers touch every day; it can fail, be copied and be stolen, and its password box can visibly disappear, so the claim is shown, not decorated.
story.object: the password box on a phone sign-in screen
story.spine: Every day you type a password that fails. Because it is the same everywhere, one leak hands a thief the key to your bank. Then the box is replaced by your fingerprint, which signs in more often. Until finally every phone signs in with no password at all.
story.ending: A wall of phones lights up one by one, each showing a passkey sign-in and no password box: 5 BILLION PASSKEYS.

alternates: Your phone still asks for a password, and most tries fail. Watch that little box disappear.
hook.headline: PASSWORDS WORK 13.8% OF TRIES

story.promise: the password box on your phone's sign-in screen disappears

facts.claim: Only 49% are distinct: for users hit by infostealers, in the median case only 49% of a user's passwords across different services were distinct from each other
Stolen logins opened 22%: the use of compromised credentials was an initial access vector in 22% of the breaches reviewed in the 2025 DBIR
Passkeys sign you in using just a fingerprint, face scan or other screen lock, and the biometric is never sent to Google's servers
Passkeys win 4x as often: average authentication success rate with passwords is 13.8%, while local passkey success rate is 63.8%
5 billion passkeys are now in use worldwide

beats.narration: Worse, it's the same password everywhere. In the median case, about half of yours are copies.
beats.headline: HALF YOUR PASSWORDS REPEAT

story.before: one sign-in box with one password
story.after: Sunny42 saved on bank, mail, shop and games: 4 REUSED
story.action: the host scrolls the saved list as the same password repeats

beats.narration: So one leak opens your bank too. Stolen logins started 22 percent of the breaches Verizon studied.
beats.headline: 22% OF BREACHES: STOLEN LOGINS

story.after: the SUNNY42 key opens the BANK lock
story.action: a leaked SUNNY42 key slides into the bank padlock and turns

beats.narration: A passkey has nothing to steal. You sign in with your fingerprint, and it never leaves the phone.
beats.headline: NO PASSWORD, JUST YOUR FINGER

story.before: a sign-in box waiting for a password
story.after: Use your passkey, fingerprint matched: SIGNED IN
story.action: the host presses a finger to the phone and the sign-in completes

beats.narration: And it actually works. Passkeys sign you in 64 percent of the time. Passwords manage just 14.
beats.headline: PASSKEY 63.8%, PASSWORD 13.8%

story.before: passkey and password at the start line
story.after: PASSKEY crosses the line at 63.8%, PASSWORD stuck at 13.8%
story.action: the two sign-ins race and the passkey reaches the finish

beats.narration: That's why 5 billion passkeys are already in use around the world.
beats.headline: 5 BILLION PASSKEYS IN USE

story.after: every phone lit: 5 BILLION PASSKEYS, NO PASSWORD BOX LEFT
story.action: a stamp lands on one phone and the passkey spreads to every screen

cta.narration: Turn one on for your bank today. Comment PASSKEY for the steps.
cta.headline_b: TURN ONE ON FOR YOUR BANK
